VA_COACH.WELCOME_P2: Beams travel through the beam pipe - an ultra-high-vacuum tube — until they meet at the interaction point inside ALICE.

ITS.TITLE: ITS (Inner Tracking System)
ITS.BODY: The ITS is the innermost particle tracking detector, located closest to the point where protons or heavy ions collide. It is built from extremely thin silicon sensors that record the passage of charged particles with a precision of just a few micrometres - less than the thickness of a human hair. This allows physicists to determine the exact point where particles are produced and to detect particles that decay almost immediately after their creation, before they can reach the outer detectors.
ITS.B1: determine the primary vertex with a resolution better than 100 micrometres
ITS.B2: reconstruct secondary vertices needed for charm and hyperon decays
ITS.B4: improve the momentum and angle resolution for particles reconstructed by the Time Projection Chamber (TPC)

FIT.TITLE: FIT (Fast Interaction Trigger)
FIT.BODY:
The FIT is one of the first detectors to respond after a particle collision in the ALICE experiment. It is designed to detect collisions almost instantly and provide a precise timing signal that tells the data acquisition system when an interesting event has occurred. This allows ALICE to record only the most relevant collisions while rejecting background events that are not useful for physics analysis.

In addition to its triggering role, the FIT detector measures the exact time of the collision and helps determine important properties such as the collision time and the event's centrality in heavy-ion collisions. These measurements are essential for the correct operation of other ALICE detectors, especially those that rely on precise timing, such as the TOF detector.
FIT.B1: Detect collisions in real time and trigger the data recording system.
FIT.B2: Measure the collision time with very high precision.
FIT.B3: Reject background events that are not true particle collisions.
FIT.B4: Support other detectors, such as TOF, by providing accurate timing information.

TPC.TITLE: TPC (Time Projection Chamber)
TPC.BODY: The TPC (Time Projection Chamber) is the largest tracking detector in the ALICE experiment and one of the largest gas detectors ever built for particle physics. It is filled with a carefully selected gas mixture through which charged particles travel after a collision. As they pass, they ionize the gas, leaving behind trails of free electrons. These electrons drift in a uniform electric field toward the detector's readout chambers, allowing physicists to reconstruct the particles' three-dimensional trajectories with high precision. A single heavy-ion collision can produce tens of thousands of charged particles, and the TPC is capable of recording their tracks simultaneously. Besides measuring the paths of particles, it also helps identify them by measuring how much energy they lose while passing through the gas.
TPC.B1: reconstruct particle tracks and visualize the paths of thousands of particles created in a single collision
TPC.B2: identify different types of particles by measuring how they lose energy while passing through the gas
TPC.B3: measure particle momentum, helping scientists understand their motion and interactions
TPC.B4: study the properties of the quark–gluon plasma created in high-energy heavy-ion collisions

TRD.TITLE: TRD (Transition Radiation Detector)
TRD.BODY: The TRD is a detector designed mainly to identify electrons among the many different particles produced in high-energy collisions. It uses a phenomenon called transition radiation, which occurs when a very fast charged particle passes through the boundary between two different materials and emits X-ray radiation. Electrons produce this radiation much more efficiently than heavier particles, allowing the TRD to distinguish them from particles such as pions. The TRD plays an important role in studying processes that involve electrons, including the investigation of the quark-gluon plasma created in heavy-ion collisions. By providing precise information about electron production and behavior, it helps physicists understand the conditions of matter under extreme temperatures and densities shortly after a collision.
TRD.B1: Identify electrons and separate them from other types of particles.
TRD.B2: Study electron production in high-energy proton and heavy-ion collisions.
TRD.B3: Investigate the quark-gluon plasma and the extreme conditions created after collisions.
TRD.B4: Improve event reconstruction by providing additional information about detected particles.

TOF.TITLE: TOF (Time Of Flight)
TOF.BODY: The TOF detector measures the time it takes for particles to travel from the collision point to the detector with extremely high precision. The accuracy of this measurement is around 50 picoseconds - just 50 trillionths of a second. By combining the measured travel time with the distance covered and the particle’s momentum, physicists can calculate its velocity and determine what type of particle it is. This allows the TOF detector to distinguish between different particles, such as pions, kaons, and protons, even when they are moving at speeds very close to the speed of light. The TOF system is especially important because many particles created in collisions have similar properties, and precise timing measurements provide an additional way to identify them.
TOF.B1: Measure particle velocities with extremely high precision.
TOF.B2: Identify different types of particles by comparing their time of flight and momentum.
TOF.B3: Distinguish between pions, kaons, and protons produced in collisions.
TOF.B4: Improve the understanding of particle interactions in high-energy collisions.

EMCAL.TITLE: EMCAL (Electromagnetic Calorimeter)
EMCAL.BODY:
The EMCAL measures the energy of electrons and photons produced in particle collisions. When one of these particles enters the detector, it creates an electromagnetic shower-a cascade of secondary particles that gradually deposit all of their energy inside the calorimeter. By measuring this cascade, physicists can determine the energy of the original particle with high precision.

EMCAL also plays a key role in the study of jets—collimated sprays of particles produced when high-energy quarks and gluons are created in collisions. Measuring the energy of electrons, photons, and jets helps scientists investigate how matter behaves under the extreme conditions produced inside the ALICE experiment.
EMCAL.B1: Measure the energy of electrons and photons with high precision.
EMCAL.B2: Study jets produced in high-energy collisions.
EMCAL.B3: Investigate how particles lose energy while passing through the quark-gluon plasma.

DCAL.TITLE: DCAL (Di-jet Calorimeter)
DCAL.BODY:
The DCAL is an extension of the EMCAL detector and operates on the same principle, measuring the energy of electrons and photons. Its main purpose is to increase the detector's coverage, allowing ALICE to observe more jets, especially pairs of jets produced in opposite directions during high-energy collisions.

With its larger acceptance, DCAL improves the study of di-jet events, where comparing the energies of two opposing jets reveals how they interact with the quark–gluon plasma. This extremely hot and dense state of matter filled the Universe for a tiny fraction of a second after the Big Bang, making these measurements an important tool for understanding the earliest moments of our Universe.
DCAL.B1: Extend the jet detection area of the ALICE experiment.
DCAL.B2: Study pairs of jets (di-jets) produced in opposite directions.
DCAL.B3: Investigate how jets lose energy while traveling through the quark–gluon plasma.

L3.TITLE: L3 (Solenoid Magnet)
L3.BODY:
The L3 magnet is the large solenoid that surrounds the ALICE detectors and creates a strong magnetic field along the beam axis. When a charged particle travels through this field, the Lorentz force bends its path into a curve. The direction of the bend reveals the sign of the particle’s charge, while the radius of curvature is related to its momentum: faster, higher-momentum particles bend less than slower ones.

Without the magnetic field, reconstructed tracks appear as straight lines. Turning on L3 transforms them into the curved trajectories used to measure momentum - a key step in understanding the particles produced in high-energy collisions.
L3.B1: Bend the paths of charged particles in a magnetic field.
L3.B2: Infer particle charge from the direction of track curvature.
L3.B3: Measure particle momentum from how strongly tracks bend.
L3.B4: Reveal the full curved event topology after the detector is assembled.

HOME.TITLE: Welcome to the ALICE Masterclass!
HOME.P1: The ALICE Collaboration has built a dedicated detector to exploit the unique physics potential of nucleus-nucleus collisions at LHC energies. Our aim is to study the physics of strongly interacting matter at the highest energy densities reached so far in the laboratory. In such condition, an extreme phase of matter - called the quark-gluon plasma - is formed.
HOME.P2: Our universe is thought to have been in such a primordial state for the first few millionths of a second after the Big Bang. The properties of such a phase are key issues for Quantum Chromo Dynamics, the understanding of confinement-deconfinement and chiral phase transitions.
HOME.P3: For this purpose, we are carrying out a comprehensive study of the hadrons, electrons, muons and photons produced in the collisions of heavy nuclei. ALICE is also studying proton-proton and proton-nucleus collisions both as a comparison with nucleus-nucleus collisions and in their own right.

INSTRUCTIONS_VISUAL_ANALYSIS.TITLE: Strange Particle Production
INSTRUCTIONS_VISUAL_ANALYSIS.SUBTITLE: Exercise 1: Visual inspection
INSTRUCTIONS_VISUAL_ANALYSIS.P1: The aim of the exercise is to search for strange particles produced from collisions at LHC and recorded by the ALICE experiment. Strange particles do not live long; they decay soon after their production. However, they live long enough to travel some distance (usually a few centimeters) from the interaction point (IP) from where they were produced (primary vertex). Their search is thus based on the identification of their decay products, which must originate from a common secondary vertex. Neutral strange particles, such as K0S and Λ, decay giving a characteristic decay pattern, called V0. The mother particle disappears some centimeters from the interaction point and two oppositely charged particles appear in its place, which are bent in opposite directions inside the magnetic field of the ALICE solenoid. In the following figure red tracks indicate positively charged particles; green tracks indicate negatively charged particles. The decays we will be looking for are:
INSTRUCTIONS_VISUAL_ANALYSIS.P2: We see that for a pion-pion the final state of the decay pattern is quasi-symmetric whereas in the pion-proton final state the radius of curvature of the proton is bigger than that of the pion: due to its higher mass, the proton carries most of the initial momentum.
INSTRUCTIONS_VISUAL_ANALYSIS.P3: We will also be looking for cascade decays of charged strange particles, such as the Ξ̅; this decays into π− Λ; the Λ then decays into π− and proton; the initial pion is characterized as a bachelor (single charged track) and is shown in purple. The search for V0s is based on the decay topology and the identification of the decay products; an additional confirmation of the particle identity is the calculation of its mass; this is done based on the information (mass and momentum) of the decay products.
INSTRUCTIONS_VISUAL_ANALYSIS.P4: In this exercise, you will determine the number of strange particles in 15 pp collisions at a collision energy of 7TeV particles can be identified through the topology of the their decays. When you select tracks from a V0 or Cascade, the relevant numbers (momentum in the form (px,py,pz) and mass) will automatically be sent to the Calculator interface, and the invariant mass for the current selected particles is calculated. Then you make a choice of particle type and click Add to include its mass in the graphs below.

INSTRUCTIONS_LARGE_SCALE_ANALYSIS.TITLE: Strange Particle Production
INSTRUCTIONS_LARGE_SCALE_ANALYSIS.SUBTITLE: Exercise 2: Large Scale Analysis
INSTRUCTIONS_LARGE_SCALE_ANALYSIS.P1: The event display is a powerful tool which helps check the quality of the data and their reconstruction and gives a “feeling” of what events look like. However,in real life data analysis is not done visually — that would be far too tedious and time-consuming. To analyse the millions of events that we collect daily at the LHC we run programs, and this is what you will do here, in order to look for V0s in a bigger event sample.
INSTRUCTIONS_LARGE_SCALE_ANALYSIS.P2: You will now analyse recordings from hundreds of events at once. You can see that the invariant mass is a continuous distribution – this is because the pairs of pions combined are random, not coming from a common secondary vertex and can give any value of mass. Most of them are background.
INSTRUCTIONS_LARGE_SCALE_ANALYSIS.P3: In order to find the number of particles of a certain type, for example K0S, you need to find the number of events in the peak after background subtraction. In order to fit a curve (second degree polynomial) to the background, you first choose the fit range using the slider. To fit a Gaussian distribution to the signal you also have to select the range of the peak. When you click on Fit, the fitted functions are superimposed on the histogram and you can check visually whether the fit is reasonable.If you think the fitted functions match the data well, you can push the Accept button. For the background subtraction the coefficients of the second degree polynomial are used; on the histogram; after clicking the Accept button you will get the total number of events in the peak, the number of background events and those which are signal.
